analysis.one_liner: Strengthens equal-pay enforcement so women can win damages when paid less than male coworkers.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 256-163 in its first week, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it much easier for women to win pay-discrimination cases. Employers would have to prove that any pay gap between men and women is job-related and necessary for the business, workers could collect compensatory and punitive damages, and anyone suing over pay discrimination could join a class action without signing a written consent form. It would also protect workers from being punished for asking about or sharing wages, and require federal agencies to collect employer pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than male coworkers, and their families. The bill would give them real money damages instead of just back pay, let them join class actions without individually signing on, and let them discuss wages without fear of retaliation. Employers that already pay equally, and small businesses exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, would face little new burden.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women paid less than male coworkers

how_it_helps.text: Workers who win a sex-discrimination case could collect compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference — not just the back pay the old law allowed.

An employer could no longer justify a pay gap with 'any factor other than sex'; the reason would have to be a bona fide factor like education, training, or experience that is job-related and consistent with business necessity.
Employees could not be retaliated against for asking about, discussing, or disclosing their own wages — a protection aimed at pay secrecy that keeps workers from learning they are underpaid.

Pay-discrimination cases could proceed as class actions with workers joined as plaintiffs without their written consent, making it practical to challenge company-wide patterns rather than suing one person at a time.
The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission would have to collect pay data from employers broken down by sex, race, and national origin, giving enforcers and workers a way to spot disparities.

Federal contractors would face restored Equal Opportunity Survey reporting and broader investigation methods for compensation discrimination, and small businesses would get compliance help while remaining exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay women less than men for similar work, who would face back pay plus compensatory and punitive damages, class-action exposure, and expanded legal fees including expert fees. All covered employers would take on new pay-data reporting, and taxpayers would fund up to $15 million in authorized spending for training, grants, and studies.

drawbacks.text: The bill would substantially raise litigation costs for employers: new compensatory and punitive damages, class actions that can add plaintiffs without written consent, expert fees recoverable from employers, and a 'same establishment' definition stretching to any workplaces in the same county — all of which broaden who can sue and how much is at stake.
New EEOC pay-data collection by sex, race, and national origin would add reporting burdens, though the bill directs the agency to weigh the burden on employers and design the reports efficiently.

Opponents in the House argued the bill should be amended to limit attorneys' fees, reflecting a good-faith concern that broad fee-shifting encourages litigation volume as much as wage fairness; the House rejected that change 178-240.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: stronger remedies and wage transparency for underpaid women versus higher litigation and compliance costs for employers. The bill tries to soften the burden — small businesses are exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, technical assistance is required, and the data-collection provision instructs the EEOC to minimize employer burden. The litigation-expansion provisions (punitive damages, consent-free class actions, county-wide establishment definition) are the parts a reasonable critic would target, but they are also the provisions that give a worker with a genuine claim actual leverage against an employer with more lawyers and money.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 256-163 in its first week, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, and it died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 6, 2009, the first day of the new Congress, with 200 of 253 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors.
On January 9, 2009, a Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions to limit attorneys' fees failed 178-240, with 169 of 177 voting Republicans in favor and 9 Democrats joining them.
The House then passed the bill 256-163: 246 voting Democrats for it and 3 against, with only 10 of 177 voting Republicans in favor.

Under the rule used for the vote, the bill's text was appended to H.R. 11 as new matter and H.R. 12 itself was laid on the table; on March 6, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.
The record shows no Senate action on H.R. 12 for the rest of the 111th Congress, and the bill died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay women less than men for similar work came out ahead: the new damages, class-action tools, wage-discussion protections, and pay-data reporting never took effect. Women workers gained nothing from this bill, which never became law.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress and assembled a large original cosponsor list.

for.name: 246 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, 246-3 among voting Democrats.

against.name: 160 of 178 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; only 10 of 177 voting Republicans supported the bill.

against.name: Rep. Tom Price
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to limit attorneys' fees; the motion failed 178-240.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business lobbying groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Paycheck Fairness Act, arguing it would flood employers with litigation.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 246 of 249 voting Democrats backed the bill while only 10 of 187 voting Republicans did, and the failed motion to recommit drew 9 Democratic votes against 169 Republican votes in favor.

industries.note: The bill would expose employers that pay women less to compensatory and punitive damages, consent-free class actions, expert fees, and a county-wide 'same establishment' rule. Their litigation and settlement exposure rises directly as workers' ability to recover pay differences rises.

The bill would reinstate the Equal Opportunity Survey and direct contract-compliance investigators to use the full range of tools for spotting compensation discrimination, ending narrower investigative methods. Contractors would face more scrutiny of their pay rolls.

Small businesses would be exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, and agencies would have to develop compliance assistance materials for them. The main effect on small business is new guidance rather than new liability.
